description: PROTOCOL_SPEC §9.6.3 `_config.allow_unknown` — the behaviour matrix for an unregistered top-level namespace (spec v1.46.0, apcore#118 decision D-69). BOTH halves of the `strict: false` row were inert in all three SDKs, and the fixture pins both: `allow_unknown: false` is documented as "silently ignored (not stored)" and the namespace was stored anyway, so `get()` answered for it; `allow_unknown: true` is documented as "stored, accessible, **WARN logged**" and no implementation logged anything. Fixing one without the other leaves the row half true. **Namespace mode only, by construction**: §9.6.3 is about namespaces, and a legacy document has none — its root IS the `apcore` namespace, so an unrecognised top-level key there is a framework key governed by §9.14's walk under `strict`. `strict`'s own clause (b) says it "applies in legacy mode too", which is the specification saying clause (a) does not; the last case pins that boundary so the scoping is a decision rather than an omission.

test_cases.description: Clause (a). `allow_unknown` is ignored when strict is true — §9.6.3's own comment says it is "only relevant when strict: false".
The half every implementation got right except the warning. The value is readable and the operator is told the namespace is unvalidated.
The defect. This case fails on every implementation before v1.46.0, where the namespace was stored and `get()` answered for it.

§9.6.3's matrix describes the DEFAULTS (`strict: false, allow_unknown: true`), so a document with no `_config` at all is the row that warns. Not the blanket warning §9.2.2 rejects: it fires on a condition specific to the document — there IS an unregistered namespace — never on every configuration ever loaded.
The quiet half, and the one that fails against an implementation that warns unconditionally.

A legacy document has no namespaces, so `allow_unknown: false` drops nothing and the key remains readable. Pinned so the scoping is a decision rather than an omission — an implementation that applied the field here would be treating framework keys as namespaces, which §9.14's walk already governs.

D-117. A legacy (namespace-less) document has no namespaces, so a declaration ABOUT a namespace has nothing to say about one — §9.6.3's reading, and the same scoping `legacy_mode_is_out_of_scope` already pins for `allow_unknown`.

apcore-rust consulted registered defaults in BOTH modes, so it answered a value for a key no reader of that file could see in it, and one the peers reported as absent. apcore-python and apcore-typescript seed these defaults into the data tree at load, which only happens in namespace mode, so they were already correct.

The declared default is deliberately NOT a canonical framework default: a case using, say, `executor.default_timeout` would be answered by the canonical default table in both modes and could not tell the two sources apart.

D-117 control. The SAME registration and the SAME key, read from a namespace-mode document, MUST answer.

Without it, 'the default does not answer in legacy mode' is equally satisfied by an implementation that never consults registered defaults at all — which would make the registration itself inert, the §9.1.3 shape the spec forbids elsewhere.

driver_contract.document: `input.namespace`, when non-null, is an unregistered top-level key carrying `{x: 1}`. In namespace mode the framework section lives under `apcore:` and `_config` is a top-level namespace beside it; in legacy mode both sit at the document root. `input.config` null means no `_config` block at all.
driver_contract.readable: `value_readable` is the answer to `get('<namespace>.x')` — a value when true, null/undefined/None when false. Drivers MUST read it through the SDK's public accessor, not off the parsed document.
